clinicalPearls: Caused by the larval coenurus stage of Taenia (Multiceps) species, with humans as accidental intermediate hosts after ingesting eggs shed by dogs and other canids
The coenurus is a fluid-filled bladder containing many invaginated protoscolices, distinguishing it from the single-scolex cysticercus and from hydatid cysts
Cerebral and spinal coenurosis presents with raised intracranial pressure, seizures, focal deficits or cord compression depending on cyst location
Subcutaneous and intramuscular coenuri present as slowly enlarging soft-tissue swellings, and ocular disease can threaten vision
Imaging shows a cystic lesion that may contain multiple scolices, and eosinophilia may be present
Definitive management is complete surgical excision of the cyst; anthelmintic drugs such as albendazole and corticosteroids may be adjuncts, particularly when surgery is difficult
Prevention relies on deworming dogs, safe disposal of infected sheep offal and good personal hygiene to avoid ingesting eggs
reference.pathophysiology: Taenia multiceps and related species are tapeworms whose adults inhabit the intestine of dogs and wild canids, with sheep and other herbivores as usual intermediate hosts. Humans become accidental intermediate hosts by ingesting eggs from canine faeces. Oncospheres hatch in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa and are carried in the blood to tissues, most importantly the brain, spinal cord, eye and subcutaneous tissue, where they develop into a coenurus, a large fluid-filled larval bladder studded with numerous protoscolices. The expanding cyst acts as a space-occupying lesion, causing mass effect, raised intracranial pressure, seizures or cord compression in the nervous system and progressive swelling elsewhere. Surrounding inflammation and, if the cyst ruptures, release of larval contents can intensify the local reaction.
additionalDifferentials: Hydatid disease (Echinococcus) of brain or soft tissue
Cerebral abscess or primary brain tumour
Arachnoid or other benign intracranial cyst
Sparganosis and other larval cestode infection
additionalInvestigations: MRI or CT to characterise the cystic lesion and detect internal scolices
Serology for cestode infection to help distinguish from cysticercosis and hydatid disease
Histological examination of the excised cyst confirming the multi-scolex coenurus
Ophthalmological assessment in suspected ocular disease
Cerebrospinal fluid examination where clinically appropriate
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus
Seizures or progressive focal neurological deficit
Spinal cord compression from a spinal cyst
Visual loss from an ocular or orbital coenurus
reference.prognosis: Prognosis after complete excision of an accessible cyst is favourable, but cerebral and spinal disease can cause serious morbidity and carries a guarded outlook when the cyst is inoperable or diagnosed late.
pitfalls: Mistaking a coenurus for neurocysticercosis or a hydatid cyst on imaging
Incomplete excision or intraoperative rupture provoking an inflammatory reaction and relapse
Relying on medical therapy alone for large space-occupying cysts
Overlooking the canine egg exposure history in the epidemiological assessment
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision of the coenurus cyst, especially for cerebral, spinal, ocular and accessible subcutaneous lesions
Adjunctive anthelmintic therapy with albendazole combined with corticosteroids to control peri-cyst inflammation, particularly when the cyst is inoperable or excision is incomplete
Corticosteroids and measures to lower raised intracranial pressure, with anticonvulsants for seizures in cerebral disease
Ophthalmological management for ocular coenurosis to preserve vision
Neurosurgical and infectious-diseases or tropical-medicine multidisciplinary care, with histological confirmation of the excised multi-scolex cyst
Public-health and preventive measures: deworming of dogs, safe disposal of infected offal, and hand and food hygiene to interrupt the canine-herbivore cycle
Escalate urgently for signs of raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus or spinal cord compression
